name: Xârâcùù
sweep_summary: Xârâcùù (xara1244) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Lionnet's 2018 WCCFL 36 talk on downstep in Paicî and Xârâcùù, has no online handout; its published proceedings version (Lionnet 2019, already on file under paic1239) dropped Xârâcùù entirely. Its Xârâcùù content was published as Lionnet 2025 (Diachronica 42: 406-427; open author draft lingbuzz 008033 fetched sources and read): every lexical word carries a predictable left-edge accent realized as a pitch drop after the first mora (words of 1-3 morae) or after the first bimoraic foot (4+ morae); the language is non-tonal and the accent is culminative, obligatory and demarcative — a description based on Rivierre 1978 (BSLP 73: 415-443, the sole primary phonological source, not obtainable online; high priority) plus Rivierre's 1977 Pangloss recordings. Three open first-hand Moyse-Faurie texts (1991 PL C-117 p. 306; 2004 HDR pp. 49, 87; 2015 valency chapter preprint p. 51) independently state initial-syllable accent/stress in Xârâcùù, with lower-register accents on dependents and second verbs in series (Rivierre's 'couplage'). Grace 1975 Canala dictionary (open, fetched sources) is silent on stress. Unread: Moyse-Faurie 1995 grammar (HathiTrust search-only, Cloudflare-blocked; Harvard print), Moyse-Faurie & Néchérö-Jorédié 1989 dictionary, and the 2002 Oceanic Languages sketch (print).

new_statements.quote: Every lexical word in Xârâcùù is marked by a pitch drop at the left edge of the word. This pitch drop occurs after the first mora in words of less than four morae, after the second mora in words of four morae and above. [...] The accentual pitch drop satisfies all three of the accent-defining criteria discussed in §2.4 above. As shown by Rivierre (1978), it is culminative (there may only be one per word) and obligatory (every lexical word has one [...]). It is also demarcative, as it highlights the left edge of the word – specifically the initial mora or foot. It is thus unambiguously accentual. It is also fully predictable.
new_statements.citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2025. Accent and tone: The double origin of the Paicî prosodic system. Diachronica 42(3-4): 406-427. doi:10.1075/dia.24039.lio. Author draft lingbuzz/008033 (the version read), Section 3.1 'Metrical conditioning of the Xârâcùù accent'.
new_statements.locator: §3.1, draft p. 9 (pdf p. 9); examples (14)-(16); accent-defining criteria same page; §3 intro p. 8 states the description is based mostly on Rivierre 1978 plus Rivierre & Tamai's 1977 recordings
new_statements.reading: Fixed, predictable, left-edge word accent (non-tonal language): the accent is a pitch drop (downstep) after the first mora in words of 1-3 morae and after the first bimoraic foot (second mora) in words of 4+ morae — i.e. word-initial accent with a mora/foot-conditioned realization site; one accent per lexical word. Independently corroborated first-hand by Moyse-Faurie (2004 HDR p. 49: 'chacun étant accentué sur l'initiale'; 2015: compounds 'stressed on the first syllable'; 1991 p. 306: main accent on the first syllable of the first verb). The primary description remains Rivierre 1978 (BSLP 73: 415-443), not obtained.

sources.quote: Every lexical word in Xârâcùù is marked by a pitch drop at the left edge of the word. This pitch drop occurs after the first mora in words of less than four morae, after the second mora in words of four morae and above. [...] Note that, as expected, accent is inaudible on monomoraic words in isolation, for lack of a second mora to realize the downstep. [...] (14) 2µ /bwii/ [bwi↓i] 'taro var.'; /katɔ/ [ka↓tɔ] 'support'; 3µ /ka̰mṵrṵ/ [ka̰↓mṵrṵ] 'person'; (15) 4µ /kɔrɔpaa/ [kɔrɔ↓paa] 'outrigger boat'; /pɛtɛɛtɛ/ [pɛtɛ↓ɛtɛ] 'potato'.
sources.locator: Section 3.1 'Metrical conditioning of the Xârâcùù accent', draft p. 9 (pdf p. 9); §3 intro draft p. 8; §3.2 pp. 10-12; abstract p. 1
sources.note: Xârâcùù is non-tonal with a culminative, obligatory, demarcative, fully predictable word accent realized as a pitch drop (downstep) at the LEFT edge of every lexical word: after the first mora in 1-3-mora words, after the second mora (i.e. after the first bimoraic foot, within a colon) in words of 4+ morae. Under 'coupling' (Rivierre 1978) dependents are integrated into the head's register span and keep their accent at a lower register. Lionnet's description is 'based mostly on Rivierre's (1978) published article', supplemented by his own transcription of Rivierre & Tamai's 1977 Pangloss reco…

sources.locator: Lionnet 2019 (proceedings), whole paper; Glottolog reference page https://glottolog.org/resource/reference/id/631959 (no URL, no pages)
sources.note: The 2018 talk itself has no online handout (Glottolog record carries no URL; author's papers page lists only the published version). The published proceedings paper (Lionnet 2019, on file under paic1239, read in full) retitled the work 'Tonal evidence from Paicî' and does not mention Xârâcùù at all (grep: zero hits; abstract page confirms). Its Xârâcùù half — the accentual downstep = word accent — was written up in Lionnet 2025 (Diachronica), fetched sources and read below. In Xârâcùù the 'downstep' IS the word-accent marker, so the talk is about accent placement in this language, but nothing…

sources.citation: Moyse-Faurie, Claire (2015). Valency classes in Xârâcùù (New Caledonia). In Andrej Malchukov & Bernard Comrie (eds.), Valency Classes in the World's Languages, vol. 2, 1015-1068. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. HAL preprint halshs-01477330.
sources.quote: Many of the classificatory suffixes reflect former verb forms, and probably stem from former nuclear-layer serialization. Compounds, however, now form a single phonological word stressed on the first syllable.
sources.locator: HAL preprint p. 51 (pdf p. 52), section on compound verbs with classificatory prefixes/suffixes
sources.note: Incidental but first-hand (Moyse-Faurie is the language's principal describer): a compound forms one phonological word 'stressed on the first syllable' — consistent with the left-edge accent of Rivierre/Lionnet. No general stress rule is stated in this syntax-oriented chapter.

sources.citation: Moyse-Faurie, Claire (2004). Catégorisation lexicale et problème de l'opposition verbo-nominale. Mémoire d'habilitation à diriger des recherches, Université Paris 4 Sorbonne. HAL tel-01408869.
sources.quote: p. 49: La succession Nom+verbe statif pourrait constituer un énoncé minimum, s'il ne s'en distinguait du point de vue accentuel. Ainsi, dans le cadre du syntagme, il se produit un "phénomène de couplage accentuel" (Rivierre, 1978), tandis que les mêmes termes en structure d'énoncé auront une accentuation disjointe, chacun étant accentué sur l'initiale, et à un même registre. — p. 87: Du point de vue accentuel, ils forment une entité au schéma bien particulier : on observe une chute accentuelle en cascade, l'accent principal portant sur la première syllabe du premier verbe, tandis que l'accent portant sur la première syllabe du deuxième verbe de la série se trouve à un registre inférieur à celui du premier verbe (cf. Rivierre). [EN: p. 49: The sequence Noun + stative verb could constitute a minimal utterance if it were not distinguished accentually: within the phrase an 'accentual coupling' occurs (Rivierre 1978), whereas the same words in utterance structure have disjoint accentuation, each accented on the initial (syllable) and at the same register. p. 87: Accentually they form a unit with a very particular pattern: a cascading accentual fall, the main accent on the first syllabl…
sources.locator: p. 49 (pdf p. 50), Xârâcùù noun + stative verb; p. 87 (pdf p. 88), Xârâcùù verb serialisation, fn. 25 citing Rivierre 1978 BSLP 73(1): 415-443
sources.note: First-hand statements (in a syntax-focused HDR) that Xârâcùù words are each accented on the initial syllable ('chacun étant accentué sur l'initiale'), with Rivierre's accentual coupling lowering the register of dependents; serial verbs: main accent on the first syllable of the first verb, lower-register accent on the first syllable of the second. Agrees with Lionnet 2025 / Rivierre 1978 (left-edge accent).

In Robert Blust (ed.), Currents in Pacific Linguistics: Papers on Austronesian languages and ethnolinguistics in honour of George W. Grace (Pacific Linguistics C-117), 305-320. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C117.305.
sources.quote: Verb series make up an indivisible whole and contain no relational morphemes. They share a common case frame, common modifiers, and common tense-aspect markers. As a whole, they have a special falling accent pattern: the main accent falls on the first syllable of the first verb, with an accent on a lower register on the first syllable of the second verb.2 [fn. 2:] For a description of accent in Xaracuu, see Rivierre (1978).
sources.note: First-hand: accent falls on the first syllable of each verb, with the second verb of a series at a lower register; refers to Rivierre 1978 for the accent description. Consistent with initial-edge accent.
